citation.title: Cluster-Robust Variance Estimation for Dyadic Data

standing_assumptions:
The article is Aronow, Samii and Assenova, ‘Cluster–Robust Variance Estimation for Dyadic Data’, Political Analysis 23:564–577 (2015). Printed page = PDF page + 563 (printed p. 566 is PDF p. 3). Everything quoted below and in the targets was read from the rendered page images (staged/pages/p-NN.png, checked against 200–300 dpi renderings of staged/main.pdf). Primes are transposes. The paper writes $\epsilon_d$ for the population residual and $e_d$ for the fitted (sample) residual; the two are different objects throughout.
(S1) Sampling and dyads, p. 566 (PDF p. 3): “Begin with a large population from which we take a random (i.i.d.) sample of units, with the sample members indexed by $i = 1, ..., N$ and grouped into $D = \binom{N}{2} = N(N-1)/2$ dyads. Pairs of unit indices within each dyad map to dyadic indices, $1, ..., D$, through the index function $d(i,j) = d(j,i)$, with an inverse correspondence $s(d(i,j)) = \{i,j\}$, and we assume no $d(i,i)$ type dyads.”
(S2) Regression and estimand, p. 566: “Consider a linear regression of $Y_{d(i,j)}$ on a $k$-length column vector of regressors $X_{d(i,j)}$ (which includes the constant): $$Y_{d(i,j)} = X'_{d(i,j)}\beta + \epsilon_{d(i,j)},$$ where $\beta$ is the slope that we would obtain if we could fit this model to the entire population, allowing for possible non-linearity in the true relationship between $\mathrm{E}[Y_{d(i,j)}|X_{d(i,j)}]$ and $X_{d(i,j)}$, and $\epsilon_{d(i,j)}$ is the corresponding population residual.$^3$ To lighten notation, for the remainder of the discussion we use $d = d(i,j)$.” Footnote 3, p. 566: “If $\mathrm{E}[Y_{d(i,j)}|X_{d(i,j)}]$ is non-linear in $X_{d(i,j)}$, the population residual will itself vary in $X_{d(i,j)}$, which undermines inference that assumes that $\epsilon_{d(i,j)}$ is independent of $X_{d(i,j)}$. The agnostic regression approach avoids such an assumption.”
(S3) Estimator, p. 566: “Define the sample data as $\mathbf{X} = (X_1 ... X_D)'$ and $Y = (Y_1 ... Y_D)'$. The ordinary least squares (OLS) estimator is $$\hat\beta = (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'Y,$$ with residual $e_d = Y_d - X'_d\hat\beta$.”
(S4) Dependence, boundedness and rank, p. 566: “Since the values of $Y_d$ and $X_d$ are determined by the characteristics of the units $i$ and $j$, $\epsilon_d$ and $\epsilon_{d'}$ for dyads containing either unit $i$ or $j$ are allowed to be correlated by construction. However, by random sampling of units, $\mathrm{Cov}(\epsilon_d, \epsilon_{d'}) = 0$ for all dyads that do not share a member. The number of pairwise dependencies between $i$ and $j$ for which $\mathrm{Cov}(\epsilon_d, \epsilon_{d'}) \ne 0$ is $O(N^3)$. Let the support for $X_d$ and $Y_d$ be bounded in a finite interval and assume the usual rank conditions on $\mathbf{X}$ (Chamberlain 1982; White 1984).”
(S5) Neighbouring dyads, p. 566 (repeated on p. 573): “$\mathcal{S}(d) = \{d' \ne d\} \cap \{d' : s(d) \cap s(d') \ne \emptyset\}$, the set of dyads other than $d$ that share a member from $d$.”
(S6) Repeated dyads, p. 567 (PDF p. 4): “Formally, suppose that for each dyad $d$ observations are indexed by $t = 1, ..., T(d)$, where the $T(d)$ values are fixed and finite. Let $(Y_{dt}, X'_{dt})$ represent the data for observation $t$ from dyad $d$, $$Y_d = \begin{pmatrix} Y_{d1} \\ \vdots \\ Y_{dT(d)} \end{pmatrix} \quad\text{and}\quad X_d = \begin{pmatrix} X'_{d1} \\ \vdots \\ X'_{dT(d)} \end{pmatrix},$$ and $Y = (Y'_1 \ldots Y'_d \ldots Y'_D)'$ and $\mathbf{X} = (X'_1 \ldots X'_d \ldots X'_D)'$, that is, the stacked $Y_d$ vectors and $X_d$ matrices, and let $\beta_r$ and $\hat\beta_r$ denote, respectively, the population slope and OLS estimator as defined above but now applied to the repeated dyads data.” In this case $X_d$ is a $T(d) \times k$ matrix and $e_d$, $\epsilon_d$ are $T(d)$-vectors.
(S7) Weighted observations, Appendix D, p. 575 (PDF p. 12): “Assume weighted directed dyad observations with weights finite and fixed; denote the weight for dyad $d$ as $w_d$. Define the sample data as $\mathbf{X} = (X'_1 ... X'_D)'$ and $Y = (Y_1 ... Y_D)'$ and the matrix of weights as $\mathbf{W} = \mathrm{diag}\{w_1, \ldots, w_D\}$. Then, the weighted least squares estimator is $$\hat\beta_w = (\mathbf{X}'WX)^{-1}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{W}Y.$$” (In the display the $W$ and $X$ inside the inverse are set in italic, not bold; the meaning is $(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X})^{-1}$.) The paper does not define $\beta_w$.
(S8) Simulation design, p. 569 (PDF p. 6): “We suppose that population values obey the following: $$Y_{d(i,j)t} = \beta_0 + \beta_1|X_i - X_j| + \underbrace{\alpha_i + \alpha_j + \nu_{d(i,j)t}}_{\epsilon_{d(i,j)t}}, \qquad (4)$$ where $Y_{d(i,j)t}$ is the $t$th observed outcome for the dyad that includes units $i$ and $j$, $X_i$, $X_j$, $\alpha_i$, $\alpha_j$, and $u_{d(i,j)t}$ are independent draws from standard normal distributions, and the compound error, $\epsilon_{d(i,j)t} = \alpha_i + \alpha_j + \nu_{d(i,j)t}$, is unobserved. In the cross-sectional case, we only observe one outcome per dyad, so $t = 1$ for all observations (i.e., the $t$ subscript is extraneous for the cross-sectional case). In the repeated observations case, we have two observations per dyad, so $t = 1, 2$ for all dyads. We fix $\beta_0 = 0$ and $\beta_1 = 1$. We use OLS to estimate $\hat\beta_0$ and $\hat\beta_1$.”
(S9) Reading used by the validators (the audit's formalization of S1–S4; not printed as such). Each unit carries a characteristic $U_i$, the $U_i$ are i.i.d., and $(X_{d(i,j)}, Y_{d(i,j)}) = f(U_i, U_j)$ for one symmetric measurable $f$, with $X_d \in \mathbb{R}^k$ and $Y_d \in \mathbb{R}$ bounded. Hence collections of dyads on disjoint sets of units are independent, and all dyads have the same marginal law. $Q = \mathrm{E}[X_dX'_d]$ is nonsingular (the ‘usual rank conditions’), $\beta = Q^{-1}\mathrm{E}[X_dY_d]$ is the population least-squares projection, $\epsilon_d = Y_d - X'_d\beta$, so that $\mathrm{E}[X_d\epsilon_d] = 0$; nothing makes $\mathrm{E}[\epsilon_d|\mathbf{X}] = 0$. The limit is $N \to \infty$. For repeated dyads the reading is $\beta_r = (\sum_d \mathrm{E}[X'_dX_d])^{-1}\sum_d \mathrm{E}[X'_dY_d]$ and $\epsilon_d = Y_d - X_d\beta_r$; for weights, $\beta_w = (\sum_d w_d\mathrm{E}[X_dX'_d])^{-1}\sum_d w_d\mathrm{E}[X_dY_d]$ and $\epsilon_d = Y_d - X'_d\beta_w$.
Scope of the list. Targets are the paper's formal results (Lemma 1, Propositions 1–2, Corollaries 1–2, the logistic estimator of Appendix E) and every confirmed error whose correction changes a mathematical statement, a formula or a proof step: P018-E001, E002, E003, E004, E005, E006, E007, N001, N003, N004, N006, N010. Two findings about the reported evidence rest on exact formal arguments and are targets for that formal content only: P018-E008 (the fitted random-effects benchmark has a covariance family that excludes the covariance of design (4)) and P018-E012 (‘an order of magnitude’ against the ratios of Table 1; the validator's evidence is itself a Lean proof). Not targets: P018-E009 (a mislabelled curve in SI Figure 4), E010 (sample counts), E011 (description of a regressor), E014 and E015 (wording and reference-list misprints), N008 (a cross-reference), which are findings about figures, data, reporting and bibliography with no mathematical statement to correct; P018-E013 and N002 (clarity notes); P018-N005 and N009 (not confirmed); P018-N007, N011, N012, N013 (out of scope). Of the headline claims, P018-H1 (Lemma 1, Proposition 1), H3 (Corollaries 1–2), H4 (Appendix E) and H5 (Proposition 2) are mathematical statements and are covered by P018-T26–T29, T14 and T16; H2 is the interpretive claim of valid inference under misspecification, whose formal content is T2, T4 and T8; H6–H10 are simulation and empirical claims.

e i}\sum_{k

Then, $\hat\Sigma_r = \hat\Sigma_D + \sum_{i=1}^{N}C_i = \hat\Sigma_D + \sum_{i=1}^{N}[C_i + D_i + E_i - D_i - E_i] = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat\Sigma_{C,i} - \hat\Sigma_D - (N-2)\hat\Sigma_0$, and by linear distributivity for $(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}$, $\hat V_r = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat V_{C,i} - \hat V_D - (N-2)\hat V_0$, with $\hat V_{C,i}$, $\hat V_D$, and $\hat V_0$ as defined in the proposition.” Text after the proposition (p. 568): “$\hat V_{C,i}$ is the usual asymptotically consistent cluster–robust variance estimator (with no degrees-of-freedom adjustment) that clusters all dyads containing unit $i$ and assumes all other observations to be independent. $\hat V_D$ is the same cluster robust estimator but clustering all repeated dyad observations. $\hat V_0$ is the usual asymptotically consistent heteroskedasticity robust (HC) variance estimator that assumes all observations (even within repeated dyad groupings) are independent. canonical_claim.note: Corrected statement for P018-E007 (error, Minor: a misprinted index in an identity); repair cost: none. This is also the paper's headline result P018-H5, an exact finite-sample identity, and both fresh readers and the batch validator found it true with each non-incident unordered dyad counted once. The identity is purely algebraic: it uses nothing about least squares, sampling or boundedness, which is why the statement is given for arbitrary arrays. With one observation per dyad, $\hat\Sigma_D = \hat\Sigma_0$ and the identity reads $\hat V = \sum_i\hat V_{C,i} - (N-1)\hat V_0$ for the $\hat V$ of equation (3).

canonical_claim.note: P018-N003 is rated an error, Minor: an undisclosed finite-sample limitation; no published value is shown to be affected. Parts (c) and the data of (d) were recomputed exactly when this list was fixed; the full exact matrix of (e) is in the artifact. canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The sentence after Proposition 1 on standard errors, corrected: $\hat V$ is symmetric but need not be positive semidefinite; a standard error is defined only for a nonnegative diagonal entry; and what the asymptotic result still gives
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed: “Standard error estimates for $\hat\beta$ are obtained from the square roots of the diagonals of $\hat V$.”
Sol's smallest repair (validated.json, P018-N003), verbatim: “Qualify the sentence: For each nonnegative diagonal entry of Vhat, obtain the corresponding standard error by its square root. The estimator need not be positive semidefinite in finite samples; a negative diagonal has no real-valued standard error. Simulation summaries should report undefined-SE counts and any omission rule. If an everywhere-defined marginal estimate is desired, separately state a convention such as sqrt(max(Vhat_jj,0)); this changes the finite-sample estimator and does not guarantee coverage.”
Formal content, with every hypothesis.
(i) [Structure of the estimator] Let $N \ge 2$, let $B$ be the $N\times D$ unit-by-dyad incidence matrix ($B_{id} = 1$ if $i\in s(d)$, else 0), let $W = B'B - I_D$, and for real arrays $X_d\in\mathbb{R}^k$, $e_d\in\mathbb{R}$ let $\mathcal{S}$ be the $D\times k$ matrix with rows $e_dX'_d$ and $G = B\mathcal{S}$. Then $W_{dd'} = 1$ if $s(d)\cap s(d')\ne\emptyset$ (including $d = d'$) and 0 otherwise; the middle factor of equation (3) is $$\sum_{d=1}^{D}\Big(X_dX'_de_d^2 + \sum_{d'\in\mathcal{S}(d)}X_dX'_{d'}e_de_{d'}\Big) = \mathcal{S}'W\mathcal{S} = G'G - \mathcal{S}'\mathcal{S};$$ so $\hat V = (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}(G'G - \mathcal{S}'\mathcal{S})(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}$ is symmetric and is a difference of two positive semidefinite matrices; it need not be positive semidefinite, even with least-squares residuals and a full-rank design (P018-T17).
(ii) [Truncation keeps consistency] For real $a, b$: $|\max(a,0) - \max(b,0)| \le |a - b|$. Hence if $V_{jj} \ge 0$ and $\tilde V_{jj} = \max(\hat V_{jj}, 0)$, then $|N\tilde V_{jj} - V_{jj}| \le |N\hat V_{jj} - V_{jj}|$; so $N\hat V_{jj} - V_{jj}\overset{p}{\to}0$ implies $N\tilde V_{jj} - V_{jj}\overset{p}{\to}0$.
(iii) [Negative diagonals become rare when the limit is positive] If $V_{jj} > 0$, then $\Pr(\hat V_{jj} < 0) \le \Pr\big(|N\hat V_{jj} - V_{jj}| \ge V_{jj}\big)$, which tends to 0 when $N\hat V_{jj} - V_{jj}\overset{p}{\to}0$ with $V_{jj}$ bounded away from 0.
(iv) [Corrected sentence] The standard error estimate of the $j$-th coefficient is $\sqrt{\hat V_{jj}}$ when $\hat V_{jj}\ge0$ and is undefined otherwise.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Corollaries 1 and 2, first conclusion ($N\mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta - \beta] - V \to 0$), and the expectation and variance steps of Appendix B: exact bounded model, full rank in every sample, uniformly bounded fitted residuals, in which the least-squares slope has infinite second moment and the variance estimator infinite mean at every $N$ (the validator's construction; not in the paper)
canonical_claim.location: p. 567 (PDF p. 4), Corollary 1, first display after ‘Then, as $N\to\infty$’; p. 575 (PDF p. 12), Corollary 2, same display; pp. 573–574 (PDF pp. 10–11), Appendix B
canonical_claim.statement:
Model. Independently for each unit $i$ draw $M_i\in\{1,2,\ldots\}$ with $\Pr(M_i = m) = 2^{-m}$; given $M_i = m$, $C_i$ uniform on $\{1,\ldots,m\}$; and independent signs $A_i, B_i$ uniform on $\{-1,1\}$, independent of $(M_i, C_i)$. Let $\delta_m = \dfrac{1}{m^22^{m^2+2}}$. Call the dyad $\{i,j\}$ small if $M_i = M_j$ and $C_i\ne C_j$; let $I_{ij}$ be its indicator, $s_{ij} = \delta_m$ if the dyad is small with $M_i = M_j = m$ and $s_{ij} = 1$ otherwise, $a_{ij} = (A_i + A_j)I_{ij}$, $u_{ij} = B_i + B_j$. Each dyad has exactly two records ($T(d) = 2$): $$X_{ij,+} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\1+s_{ij}\end{pmatrix},\ Y_{ij,+} = u_{ij} + a_{ij}; \qquad X_{ij,-} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\1-s_{ij}\end{pmatrix},\ Y_{ij,-} = u_{ij} - a_{ij}.$$
(a) [Conditions] Regressors lie in $[0,2]$ and outcomes in $[-4,4]$ for all $N$. $\mathrm{E}[Y|\mathbf{X}] = 0$, so $\beta_r = (0,0)'$ and the population residual is $Y$. With $q = \mathrm{E}[s_{12}^2]$, $\tfrac23\le q\le1$, and the population Gram matrix per record is $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1+q\end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $q > 0$.
(b) [Full rank in every sample] With $S = \sum_{i<j}s_{ij}^2 > 0$, $\det(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}) = 4DS > 0$ for every sample and every $N \ge 2$.
(c) [Exact least squares] Writing the slope coefficient as $\hat b$ and $\bar B = N^{-1}\sum_iB_i$: $\hat b = \dfrac{\sum_{i<j}s_{ij}a_{ij}}{S}$, the intercept is $2\bar B - \hat b$, and $e_{ij,\pm} = B_i + B_j - 2\bar B \pm(a_{ij} - \hat bs_{ij})$. For every $N \ge 2$ and every sample, $|e_{ij,\pm}| \le 8$.
(d) [Infinite second moment] Fix $N \ge 3$. For $m \ge N$ let $E_m = \{M_i = m\text{ for all } i,\ C_1,\ldots,C_N\text{ distinct}\}$. Then $\Pr(E_m) = 2^{-mN}\dfrac{m(m-1)\cdots(m-N+1)}{m^N}$, and on $E_m$: $\hat b = 2\bar A/\delta_m$ with $\bar A = N^{-1}\sum_iA_i$, $\mathrm{E}[\hat b^2|E_m] = \dfrac{4}{N\delta_m^2}$. For $m \ge N(N-1)$, $$\mathrm{E}\big[\hat b^2\mathbf{1}_{E_m}\big] \ge \frac{32}{N}m^42^{2m^2 - mN} \ge 2^{m^2}.$$ Hence $\mathrm{E}[\hat b^2] = +\infty$ for every $N \ge 3$ (and $\mathrm{E}|\hat b| = +\infty$): $\mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta_r - \beta_r]$ is not finite, and the first conclusion of Corollary 1 fails for every target $V_r$.
(e) [The variance estimator] The slope diagonal entry of the printed $\hat V_r$ is $\hat V_{22} = S^{-2}\sum_{(d,d'):\,s(d)\cap s(d')\ne\emptyset}s_ds_{d'}r_dr_{d'}$ with $r_d = a_d - \hat bs_d$. On $E_m$, with $S_A = \sum_i(A_i - \bar A)^2$, $$\hat V_{22} = \frac{(N-2)(N-3)S_A}{D^2\delta_m^2}, \qquad \mathrm{E}[S_A] = N - 1 .$$ On the complement of $\bigcup_mE_m$, $|\hat V_{22}| \le 16D^2$. Hence $\mathrm{E}[\hat V_{22}] = +\infty$ for every $N \ge 4$; neither $\mathrm{E}[N\hat V_r]$ nor $\mathrm{Var}[N\hat V_r]$ is finite.
(f) [The asymptotic statements hold] With $h_m = 2^{-m}(1 - 1/m)\delta_m$, $H = \sum_{m\ge1}2^{-3m}(1-1/m)^2\delta_m^2\in(0,\infty)$ and $v = 4H/q^2 > 0$: $\sqrt N(\hat\beta_r - \beta_r)\Rightarrow\mathcal{N}(0, V_\infty)$ and $N\hat V_r\overset{p}{\to}V_\infty$, where $V_\infty = \begin{pmatrix}4+v&-v\\-v&v\end{pmatrix}$ is positive definite.
(g) [Corollary 2] Giving each unit an auxiliary independent uniform $U_i$ and assigning the $+$ record to the direction from smaller to larger $U$ and the $-$ record to the reverse direction makes the records directed observations with all weights 1; $\hat\beta_w = \hat\beta_r$ and $\hat V_w = \hat V_r$, so (d)–(f) apply to Corollary 2.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Corollary 1, Corollary 2 and their estimators as printed: P018-T28, P018-T29. Repeated and weighted settings: (S6), (S7). Appendix B, conditions (i)–(ii): P018-T27. The symbols $M_i$, $C_i$, $A_i$, $B_i$, $\delta_m$, $s_{ij}$, $a_{ij}$, $u_{ij}$, $E_m$, $S$, $S_A$ belong to this target only ($S$ is not the score sum of other targets; $s_{ij}$ is not the paper's $s(d)$; $C_i$, $E_m$ are not the $C_i$, $E_i$ of Appendix C). In (c) the bound $|e|\le8$ is the validator's (derivation, section 4), by a count of small and non-small pairs. In (d): $\delta_m^{-2} = m^42^{2m^2+4}$ and the probability that $N$ uniform draws from $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ are distinct is at least $\tfrac12$ when $m\ge N(N-1)$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: (a)–(e) are exact for each fixed $N$; (f) is a limit statement, proved in the validator's derivation (section 7) by the projection argument of P018-T8 and the count of P018-T4.
canonical_claim.note: P018-N004 is rated an error, Minor: the claim has to be restated for the variance of the limiting distribution or given a moment condition; inference survives. A second model in the artifact (runs/P018/validate/P018-N004/v1/artifact/scalar_derivation.md), with one record per unordered dyad, bounded data, residuals bounded by 100 and almost surely full rank, has $\mathrm{E}|\hat V_{22}| = \mathrm{E}[\hat V_{22}^2] = \infty$ for every $N \ge 5$; it shows that the moment route of Appendix B fails in the setting of Proposition 1 itself and is not required of the formalizer. The model satisfies the rank conditions the paper describes and uses; the works cited for ‘the usual rank conditions’ were not available to the validator.
